page3_img_2.png.title: Survey constructs and their theoretical instruments
page3_img_2.png.description: A two-column table listing the survey’s measured constructs (left) and the validated theoretical instruments used to operationalize them (right). The four core appraisal drivers—Value, Identity, Accountability, and Demands—are mapped to the Job Characteristics Model, Self‑Determination Theory, Felt Accountability, and the Job Demands‑Resources Model, respectively. Outcome and moderator measures are also shown: Openness to AI Support uses the Levels of Automation framework, AI Usage uses the UTAUT technology‑acceptance model, and Risk Tolerance/Technophilia use the Cognitive Style Facet Survey. These mappings indicate how the paper grounded its predictors, outcomes, and individual‑difference moderators in established theory when fitting mixed‑effects models linking appraisals to AI openness and use.

page3_img_1.png.title: Grounded taxonomy of software-engineering task categories and example tasks
page3_img_1.png.description: A two-column table enumerating five top-level SE task categories and representative tasks used in the survey. Categories are Development (e.g., coding/programming, bug fixing/debugging, performance optimization, refactoring & maintenance/updates, AI integration); Design & Planning (system design, requirements engineering, project planning & management); Quality & Risk Management (testing & QA; code review/pull requests; security & compliance); Infrastructure & Operations (DevOps/CI‑CD, environment setup & maintenance, infrastructure monitoring, customer support); and Meta‑work (Collaboration & Knowledge Building) (documentation; client/stakeholder communication; mentoring & onboarding; learning, research & brainstorming). The paper used this taxonomy to present category-specific appraisal blocks: respondents picked 2–3 of these categories for detailed ratings of value, identity, accountability, demands and for prioritizing Responsible AI principles.

page4_img_1.png.title: Mixed-effects regression: appraisals predicting openness to and use of AI
page4_img_1.png.description: A two-column table of standardized mixed-effects regression results predicting (left) developers’ openness to AI support and (right) reported AI usage from four task-appraisal predictors and experience controls. Value, Accountability, and Demands all have positive, highly significant coefficients for both outcomes (e.g., Value β = .12***, d = .16 for openness; β = .16***, d = .18 for usage), while Identity shows a negative, significant association with openness (β = -.09***, d = -.15) but a positive association with usage (β = .15***, d = .20). SE experience is negatively associated with reported usage (β = -.09***, d = -.13) whereas AI experience has a large positive association (openness β = .19***, d = .27; usage β = .41***, d = .46). Model fit (marginal/conditional R2) is reported (.25/.45 for openness; .25/.48 for usage) and the analysis is based on 10,449 observations; significance levels are noted in the table footnote (*** p < .001).

page7_img_1.png.title: Quadrant map of SE tasks: AI support need vs. current usage
page7_img_1.png.description: Scatterplot maps SE tasks by standardized openness-to-AI (x-axis) and reported AI usage (y-axis); points are z-scores relative to the sample mean and are color/shape coded by cluster (green circles = Core Work, blue triangles = People & AI Building, orange hexes = Ops & Coordination). Quadrants are labeled Improve (high need, high use), Build (high need, low use), Sustain (low need, high use), and De-prioritize (low need, low use). Examples show Coding and Bug Fixing in the Improve quadrant (high openness and high AI use), Testing/QA and Refactoring/Maintenance toward high openness (right side) with varying usage, while DevOps, environment setup, infrastructure monitoring, and Documentation appear in the Build quadrant (high need but lower current use), indicating gaps to address. Relational and strategic tasks—Mentoring and Stakeholder Communication—sit in the De-prioritize quadrant (low need and low use), and System Design/Requirements lie left of center in the Sustain area, reflecting modest AI need but some existing use.

page8_img_1.png.title: Developers’ top Responsible AI priorities by task category
page8_img_1.png.description: Bar chart showing the percentage of participants (forced to pick their top‑5 RAI principles) who prioritized eight Responsible AI principles across five task categories (Development, Design & Planning, Quality & Risk, Infra & Ops, Meta‑work). Reliability & Safety (≈80–90%) and Privacy & Security (≈70–85%) are the most selected across all categories, followed by Transparency and Goal Maintenance (both roughly mid‑60s to mid‑70s%). AI Accountability and Steerability sit in the mid‑60% range, while Fairness and Inclusiveness are least selected overall (~30%); however, meta‑work (blue bars) shows noticeably higher selection of Fairness and Inclusiveness (~40–45%). Small error bars indicate consistency across respondents; these patterns align with the paper’s finding that systems‑facing tasks prioritize reliability/security, whereas human‑facing/meta tasks elevate fairness and inclusiveness.

page9_img_1.png.title: Odds ratios from GLMMs predicting prioritized Responsible AI principles
page9_img_1.png.description: This table reports baseline odds (for development tasks) and odds ratios from logistic mixed-effects models predicting whether developers selected each Responsible AI (RAI) principle (columns: Reliability & Safety; Privacy & Security; Transparency; Goal Maintenance; Steerability; AI Accountability; Fairness; Inclusiveness) as a top‑5 priority. Baseline odds are highest for Reliability & Safety (18.15 ≈ 95% probability), followed by Privacy & Security (8.19 ≈ 89%), Transparency (5.17 ≈ 84%), Goal Maintenance (4.68), Steerability (3.65) and AI Accountability (3.03), while Fairness and Inclusiveness have low baseline odds (~0.21 and 0.20). Task‑level effects: Design & Planning lowers odds of prioritizing Reliability (OR=0.49) but raises Goal Maintenance (OR=1.45) and Fairness/Inclusiveness (OR≈1.48/1.61); Quality & Risk Management and Infrastructure & Operations increase odds of prioritizing Privacy & Security (OR≈1.91 and 1.38 respectively); Meta‑work strongly increases Fairness and Inclusiveness (OR≈3.06 and 2.49). Individual differences matter: greater SE experience, AI experience, risk tolerance, and technophilia raise odds of prioritizing Steerability (and relatedly Reliability or Transparency in some cases)—e.g., SE experience (OR≈1.15 for Reliability; 1.21 for Steerability), AI experience (OR≈1.30 for Transparency), and technophilia (OR≈1.16 for Goal Maintenance, 1.28 for Steerability). Model fit (Rm2/Rc2) indicates fixed effects explain modest variance while participant‑level random effects add substantial explanatory power; p‑values were FDR‑adjusted.

page6_img_table_1.png.title: Task appraisal table: Value, Identity, Accountability, and Demand across SE tasks
page6_img_table_1.png.description: A multi-column table summarizing developers’ percent‑agree ratings (4–5 on a 5‑point scale) and ranks for four appraisal drivers—Task Value, Task Identity, Task Accountability, and Task Demand—for 20 software‑engineering tasks grouped into three clusters (Cluster 1: Core Work; Cluster 2: People & AI Building; Cluster 3: Ops & Coordination). Key numbers: Coding/Programming scores highest in Value (98.0%, rank #1), Identity (97.0, #1) and Accountability (94.9, #1); System Design and Performance Optimization top Task Demand (90.7% and 89.5%, ranks #1 and #2). In contrast, Ops & Coordination items (e.g., Documentation 31.4% identity, Stakeholder Communication 35.0%) show much lower identity alignment despite moderately high Value (documentation 85.4% value). The table thus concretely supports the paper’s cluster interpretation: Core Work combines very high value, accountability and demand (and often high identity), People & AI‑Building is identity‑heavy but lower in value, and Ops & Coordination has respectable value/demand but weak identity.
